But if we present things systematically, Ontology comes first and Cosmology second. From that systematic point of view, Phenomenology ought to come only after Cosmology.

We would first show in Ontology what Being is and explain why—that is, how—it exists. We would then describe this existence in Cosmology and explain why it “appears” in the way it actually appears. From there it would be natural to describe this appearance itself, and so arrive at Phenomenology.
Yet, as we already know and will see again, Phenomenology is an introduction to Philosophy. It is therefore simultaneously an introduction to Ontology and Cosmology.
Within the overall system it comes before Philosophy in the narrower sense.
Philosophy in the broad sense thus divides first into Phenomenology and systematic Philosophy, while systematic Philosophy in turn divides into Ontology and Cosmology.

But it studies them with Cosmology and Ontology already in view. It describes phenomena in such a way that we can move directly from their phenomenological description to a cosmological and ontological investigation of the world that appears and of the Being that exists in that world.
The phenomenologist therefore knows from the beginning what philosophy is, because he describes “phenomena” from the philosophical point of view.
In that sense, he is already a philosopher.
But at the same time, he knows that he becomes a philosopher only at the end of Phenomenology and through Phenomenology.
Only at the end will he truly know what philosophy is, because the philosophical point of view—his own point of view—emerges only there.
Phenomenology is therefore the last “phenomenon” described by the phenomenologist.
Yet from the very beginning he describes every phenomenon—not just Phenomenology itself—from a phenomenological and therefore philosophical point of view.
In this sense, the whole of Phenomenology is a philosophical science: the philosophical science of phenomena.
That is why it can be treated as a part of Philosophy in the broad sense—the first and introductory part—on the same level as the Ontology and Cosmology that make up systematic Philosophy.
As I have already said, Phenomenology is a philosophical science because it describes its object—the phenomenon—completely, without abstracting from anything.
For this reason, its description also makes it possible to move beyond phenomena and understand their “cause.”
From the beginning, Phenomenology looks at phenomena, so to speak, from the outside.
It can therefore, on the one hand, describe each phenomenon completely and, on the other, look at what lies behind it.
The ordinary person and the scientist describe only a part of the phenomenon, without knowing that what they describe is only one part of a whole and that this whole is precisely the phenomenon.
They therefore cannot even formulate the cosmological and ontological question about the cause of the phenomenon as such.
When they look for the cause of one part of a phenomenon, they simply encounter another part of a phenomenon—that is, another phenomenon.
They discover only something that appears to a particular person in a particular way, without relating it to the person to whom it appears or to the way it appears.
Phenomenology, by contrast, begins by considering the phenomenon as a whole: not only what appears, but also how it appears and to whom.
For this reason, Phenomenology prepares us to ask about the cosmological world that appears as it appears to the person to whom it appears.
That is, it prepares us to ask about the world that serves as the “cause” of each phenomenon taken as a whole, and of all possible phenomena in general.
It is the world—and, through the world, Being—that “manifests itself,” not “appearance” itself.
The appearance is certainly given in some sense to the phenomenologist, since he speaks about it.
But the “phenomenon” does not itself “appear” to the phenomenologist any more than the “cosmos” appears to the cosmologist or “Being” appears to the ontologist.
The reason is the same in every case.

On the one hand, the “phenomenon”—considered as phenomenon, rather than as what appears within it; the appearing of the birch rather than the “birch that appears”—is not given to just anyone in just any way. It is given only to the philosopher, the phenomenologist, and only in a philosophical or phenomenological way.
On the other hand, this philosophical or phenomenological “given” already includes the way in which it is given and the person to whom it is given.
Phenomenology describes not only the phenomena themselves but also the way in which they are given. In that sense, it describes itself as Phenomenology.
And it also describes the person to whom they are given—that is, its own author.
The author of a Phenomenology is a living human being, and the Phenomenology itself is a book—thought through, written, and published.
So Phenomenology itself also becomes a “phenomenon”: something that can “manifest itself” to someone in all sorts of ways.

To a child or to a “savage,” for example, it might appear merely as sheets of paper and a chemical body, as difficult or completely incomprehensible speech, as the subject of an obscure scholarly investigation, and so forth.
Phenomenology itself, then, is described within Phenomenology as its final phenomenon.
But precisely because Phenomenology includes itself as a phenomenon, it is not merely a phenomenon.

Its author and its reader—at least a reader who has understood it—know that Phenomenology, as book or discourse, appears to them. They know how it appears to them. And they know who they themselves are, the people to whom it appears.
In this sense, once they have completed the Phenomenology—whether by writing it or reading it—it is no longer merely a phenomenon for them.
And for the same reason, the appearance described within it is no longer merely “phenomenal.”
This means that through Phenomenology its author and reader have become philosophers.
They now deal no longer merely with “appearances” but with the actuality that appears—to anyone and in any way, but in particular to them and in a phenomenological way.
In other words, they now deal with the cosmos studied by the cosmologist.
The only difference is that the phenomenologist describes this cosmos as phenomenon, whereas the cosmologist studies the world as the cause of that phenomenon.
If we like, Phenomenology is an appearance appearing to itself.
But an appearance that appears to itself is no longer merely an appearance. It is the world appearing to itself.
Phenomenology speaks about the appearing of this world. Cosmology speaks about the world that appears.
In this sense, the cosmologist returns, so to speak, to the perspective of the ordinary person or scientist.
Like them, he speaks not about the appearing of the world but about the world.
The difference is that the ordinary person and scientist do not know that this world “appears,” to whom it appears, or how it appears.
The cosmologist, by contrast, speaks of the world as the cause of its own appearing.
For that reason he does not speak about abstractions but about concrete reality.
And he can speak in this way only because Phenomenology has already spoken about concrete appearing, shown him what it is, and thereby made it possible for him to ask about its cause.
We can therefore state the point once more.

The ordinary person and the scientist speak about the “objects” that “appear” to them. But they forget that those objects appear, and consequently speak about them without asking how they appear or to whom.
The phenomenologist speaks about the appearance itself.
That means he speaks not only about the object that appears, but also about the way it appears and the person to whom it appears.
This “object”—an object appearing in a particular way to a particular person—is called a phenomenon or appearance (Erscheinung).
In our example, the phenomenon is therefore not simply “the birch.” It is the birch as perceived in a certain way by a certain person.
The way in which this object appears is called its cognition or experience (Erfahrung).
So in our example, this cognition is not simply “sensory perception in general,” but the sensory perception of this particular birch by this particular person.
Finally, the one to whom the object appears is called consciousness (Bewusstsein).
In our example, consciousness is not “the human being in general,” but this particular human being insofar as he sensorially perceives this particular birch.
It is therefore precisely the consciousness of the birch, not the complete human being taken as a whole.

Whenever Phenomenology speaks of a “phenomenon” or “appearance”—that is, of an appearing object—it therefore always relates that phenomenon, on the one hand, to its cognition or experience, through which the object appears, and, on the other hand, to the consciousness to which the object appears.
Taken together as a single whole, phenomenon, cognition, and consciousness are no longer merely an “appearance.” Together they constitute reality itself.

Yet this consciousness is consciousness only of the phenomenon through cognition; cognition is cognition only of the phenomenon through consciousness; and the phenomenon is the appearance of reality to a consciousness through cognition.
So the phenomenologist considers this reality precisely in its character as appearance or phenomenon.
He describes the way a reality appears to itself through cognition to a consciousness, and therefore appears as a phenomenon.
But once he has described this phenomenon, the phenomenologist naturally asks what this reality is that “makes itself appear” in this way to a consciousness through cognition.
He asks what this cognition is through which reality appears in this way to consciousness.
And he asks what this consciousness is to which reality appears in this way through cognition.
In other words, he searches for the cause of the phenomenon.
And he finds it in the human being in the world studied by the cosmologist.

But once he begins speaking about the human being who, through cognition and within consciousness, makes both the world and himself appear, and about the world that appears through humanity, the phenomenologist ceases to be merely a phenomenologist.
He becomes a cosmologist—that is, a philosopher.

Phenomenology therefore presents itself from the outset as a philosophical science. For that reason, it has nothing to do with what we ordinarily call “science.” In particular, it differs fundamentally and radically from scientific psychology and scientific history.

As a philosophical science, Phenomenology is not “abstract” but “concrete.” When the phenomenologist studies an “object,” he does not set aside the questions of how and through what means that object is given to him, or who he himself is—in other words, who this person is to whom the object is given in this particular way.

Taken as a whole, then, the text of the Phenomenology—its entire subject matter—does more than give a complete description of its “object.” It also explains how its own particular way of knowing that object is possible, and it answers the question of who its author is: who is this phenomenological “consciousness” to which a phenomenological object becomes “given” through a phenomenological form of cognition?

More simply, Phenomenology includes within its description of what it describes an account of how it describes it and of who is doing the describing. Alongside its object, its subject matter therefore includes both itself and its author.

Ordinary “science,” by contrast—and psychology and history in particular—limits itself to describing its “objects.” Its subject matter coincides with its object, or more exactly, consists only in a description of that object. The question of how the object is given, and to whom, lies outside the field of inquiry.

Yet an object must in fact be given to some particular person in some particular way if it is ever to become the subject of a description. “Science” forgets this and therefore imagines that it is describing the “object” simply as it exists “in reality.”
But precisely because it thinks this way, while forgetting that the object is given in a particular way to a particular person, science actually describes only how that object appears to it.

Science thinks it is dealing with “reality itself”—in effect, mistakenly taking itself for a kind of Cosmology. But what it actually deals with are “phenomena,” and these are what it describes. A “phenomenon,” however—and the unconscious, scientific description of it—is determined not only by the object that appears, but also by the way it appears and by the person to whom it appears.

A particular science therefore describes, on the one hand, only a particular aspect of its object: specifically, the aspect revealed by the particular form of cognition characteristic of that science. On the other hand, it describes only the aspect given to a particular observer—to the consciousness of the person who created that science.

And this consciousness is determined not only by what is given to it, but also by the kind of human being who embodies it—that is, by that person’s individual interests and class interests. In this sense, “science” itself appears as a social ideology: a class opinion, rather than knowledge in the full sense of the word.
So “science,” without realizing it, describes isolated ideological aspects of reality—or of the cosmos, meaning the world in the broadest sense.

Phenomenology is different. Because it takes account both of how reality is given and of the person to whom it is given, it deals, in principle, with reality itself rather than with isolated ideological aspects of reality.
